title: Whither quantum advantage? New classical lower bounds for Max-Cut on large-girth 3-regular graphs
authors: Flaviano Morone, Shivang Rawat, Dries Sels
abstract: Every 3-regular graph of girth at least $g$ has a cut containing at least a fraction $M_g$ of its edges, and the best rigorous bounds at large girth are $0.912\le \lim_{g\to\infty}M_g \le 0.92386$. Lower bounds on $M_g$ follow from the performance of local algorithms: on a graph of girth $g \ge 2p+2$ a depth-$p$ local algorithm sees the same tree around every edge, so its expected cut fraction on that tree bounds $M_g$ from below. We apply this strategy to the Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL), a classical local algorithm, and evaluate it on the depth-$p$ tree for every even depth up to $p=32$. The resulting bounds exceed those recently obtained from the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for every $p\ge 4$, by $0.005$ to $0.011$, and they extend the range of girths covered from $g=36$ to $g=66$. Notably, at $g=66$ we obtain $M_{66} \ge 0.9127$ at $99.99999\%$ confidence level, which raises the asymptotic lower bound from $0.912$ to $0.9127$.
summary: This paper investigates the Max-Cut problem on large-girth 3-regular graphs to test for quantum advantage. By analyzing the local structure using a classical algorithm called VIRAL, the authors derive rigorous lower bounds on the maximum cut fraction. These classical bounds surpass those from the QAOA for moderate depths, suggesting that quantum computation may not offer an exponential advantage for this specific optimization task.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the maximum cut fraction ($M_g$) for 3-regular graphs with large girth ($g$), challenging the notion of quantum advantage in optimization.
main_result: A classical local algorithm (VIRAL) provides rigorous lower bounds for $M_g$ that exceed those obtained from the QAOA for depths $p \ge 4$, suggesting quantum advantage may not exist for this problem.
method: The authors analyze the expected cut fraction on the tree structure formed by the radius-$p$ neighborhood of an edge, using the Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL) to establish these bounds.
model_or_system: The model is the Max-Cut problem applied to 3-regular graphs, specifically focusing on the behavior of these graphs as their girth ($g$) becomes very large. The analysis relies on the local structure (tree approximation) around any given edge.
key_observables: The maximum cut fraction $M_g$, and the derived lower bound $c_{	ext{VIRAL}}(p)$ based on the depth-$p$ tree structure.
important_parameters: The depth parameter $p$ (related to girth $g$ by $g \ge 2p+2$), and the confidence level used for statistical bounding (e.g., 99.99999%).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that for large girth, the local structure around any edge can be accurately modeled by a tree, allowing the cut fraction to be determined by local algorithms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of the radius-2 neighborhood of an edge in a 3-regular graph, and plots compare the cut fraction achieved by VIRAL, QAOA, and TPM across different depths.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for $M_g$ using local algorithms, applies the VIRAL algorithm to the depth-$p$ tree, compares its resulting bounds against established quantum (QAOA) and classical benchmarks (TPM), and concludes that classical methods match or exceed quantum performance.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the question of quantum advantage for combinatorial optimization problems like Max-Cut, providing concrete evidence that classical local algorithms can match or surpass current quantum algorithm performance on structured graphs.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Section of a 3-regular graph of girth g ≥6. The radius-2 neighborhood of an edge (u, v), consisting of the 14 vertices within distance 2 of u or v, and the 13 edges incident to u, v and their neighbors. The girth forces this tree structure. Any further edge among these vertices must join two leaves (since every other vertex already has degree 3) and it is allowed only if the two leaves lie on opposite sides of (u, v), where it closes a cycle of length 6 (dashed edge).

Inset: p ≥20, with the lower confidence bound L of Table I (open circles), which crosses 0.912 at p = 32. Lines are guides to the eye.

FIG. 3. VIRAL with p = 2 layers on the graph of Fig. 1 traced backwards from the output. (a), The cut variables σu, σv need su(2) and sv(2). (b), Through Eq. (3) these need the states at n = 1 of u, v and their four other neighbors a1, a2, b1, b2. No state of a leaf is needed at n = 1 or n = 2. (c), These six states need the seeds of all 14 vertices. The leaves enter only through their seeds, so the edges joining two leaves, such as the dashed one, play no role. Hence (σu, σv) is a fixed function of the 14 i.i.d. seeds on the tree of Fig. 1, the same for every edge of every 3-regular graph of girth g ≥6.
